answer: Sunlight has many colors, like a rainbow. Tiny bits of air scatter blue light in all directions, so the sky looks blue.
Grass has a green helper called chlorophyll that catches sunlight. Think of each blade as a little solar panel that helps the grass make food.
Sleep gives your body time to rest and your brain time to sort what you learned. It is a bit like putting your toys back in their boxes after playing.
Rivers carry tiny bits of salt from rocks into the sea. When water rises into the air, the salt stays behind, a little like salt left in a bowl after water dries.
Clouds are full of tiny drops of water that bump together and grow. When they get heavy enough, they fall like drops from a wet sponge.
Stars are huge balls of hot gas that make their own light. They look like tiny lights because most are very far away. The Sun is our closest star.
The Moon shines because sunlight bounces off its surface. Think of it like a ball lit by a flashlight.
Earth spins like a top. When your part faces the Sun it is day, and when it turns away it is night.
Plants use sunlight, air, and water to make food and grow. Their roots take in water like little drinking straws.
Clouds are made of tiny drops of water or bits of ice. A cloud is a little like fog floating high above the ground.
When water gets cold enough, its tiny pieces slow down and lock together to make ice. Think of loose building blocks snapping into a solid shape.
When sunlight passes through raindrops, the drops spread its colors out. Each drop is a bit like a tiny piece of shiny glass.
Dogs let heat out when they pant. Moving air over their wet tongues cools them a little, like a breeze on damp skin.
A cat makes a purr by moving parts in its throat as it breathes. Cats often purr when relaxed, a little like a quiet motor.
Birds push air down with their wings, and the air pushes the birds up. You can think of their wings as paddles that push against the air.
Fish pass water over their gills, which pick up oxygen from the water. Gills do a job a little like your lungs, but in water.
Bees can make a buzz by moving their wings very fast. The quick movements shake the air, like a tiny drum beating very quickly.
A caterpillar changes inside a shell called a chrysalis. When that change is done, a butterfly comes out with wings.
Your heart squeezes to push blood through your body. It works like a little pump that keeps moving while you work, play, or sleep.
Your bones hold your body up and protect parts inside you. Together, they make a frame a bit like the beams that hold up a house.
Sound makes the air wiggle, and those wiggles move a thin part inside your ear. Your ear and brain work together to tell you what made the sound.
An echo happens when sound bounces off something and comes back to you. It is like rolling a ball toward a wall and watching it bounce back.
A sneeze is a quick blast of air that can clear dust from your nose. It is like your nose’s own little cleaning puff.
Lightning heats the air around it very quickly. That air pushes outward, making the loud sound we call thunder.
Snow starts as tiny bits of ice inside clouds. More ice sticks to them as they grow, like little building blocks making a pattern.
Sunlight warms some places more than others. Air moves as warmer air rises, and that moving air is wind.
Water in a puddle can turn into a gas and mix with the air. That is why a puddle grows smaller like wet clothes drying on a line.
A candle flame gets its fuel from melted wax that moves up the wick. The wick is like a tiny straw that brings wax to the flame.
Saturn’s rings are made of many pieces of ice and rock moving around the planet. From far away, those pieces look like wide, bright bands.
Gravity pulls things toward Earth. It is like an invisible tug that keeps your feet on the ground and brings a dropped ball back down.
